label: Figure 2
title: What predicts voluntary turnover: corrected correlations from 316 studies
caption: Eighteen predictors of voluntary turnover from the 2018 meta-analysis by Rubenstein, Eberly, Lee and Mitchell, drawn from 316 articles with a mean lag of about 16 months, most samples from the United States [178](#cite:178). Withdrawal cognitions (.56) and job search (.40) are the strongest; commitment, fit, satisfaction and embeddedness run between −.26 and −.29; pay is −.17 and workload −.10 [178](#cite:178).
how_to_read: Bars to the right mean more of the predictor goes with more quitting; bars to the left mean more of it goes with less quitting. The number beside each bar in the data file, k, is how many studies it rests on; a bar built on four studies (engagement) is less settled than one built on 211 (withdrawal cognitions). The retain-stage records are ordered by this chart.

explain.text: Thinking about quitting and intending to; the strongest predictor at .56 across 211 studies [178](#cite:178).
The links, fit and sacrifices that hold a person in place; −.26 across 29 studies [178](#cite:178).
Pay level correlates −.17 with quitting, weaker than the attitudes above it; the peer-comparison evidence in the offer and retain records explains part of why [178](#cite:178).

source: Correlations and k are as published in the meta-analysis as the pack recorded them [178](#cite:178); no re-analysis. Climate and engagement rest on few studies and are shown as reported.
provenance: synthesised from data across cited works
